Snack time?
Picture a pond on a warm night.
Frogs sit at the edge of the water, waiting.
For a frog, the rules of dinner are simple.
If something small moves,
you shoot out your tongue,
and the insect is gone.
Frogs have hunted this way for
millions of years, and insects
have paid the price.
Beetles, flies, crickets, and caterpillars
all end up on the menu.
But what happens when one insect
refuses to play the victim?
Today, we meet a beetle that turns
that rule upside down.
On the food web diagrams in school
books, the arrow points one way,
from the insect to the frog.
Predator and prey, and no confusion
about which is which.
In damp places across the Old World,
from Africa to the Mediterranean
and into Asia, there lives a beetle
larva that grows to only about
two centimeters long.
It is slim and soft-looking,
pale yellow or white,
with black and orange markings.
To a passing frog,
it looks like the easiest midnight
snack in the world.
But this larva is not waiting to be eaten.
It is waiting for something else.
It is waiting for the frog.
You could walk past one on a
damp night and never notice it
under the leaves.
Meet Epomis, a genus of ground
beetles with about thirty species.
Ground beetles are one of the largest
beetle families on Earth,
with about 40,000 known species,
and most of them hunt small invertebrates
like worms, snails, and caterpillars.
Epomis larvae are different.
They feed only on amphibians:
frogs, toads, newts, and salamanders.
And they feed on living animals
much larger than themselves.
Scientists call this a predator-prey
role reversal.
So how does a creature smaller
than your thumb pull it off?
To answer that, we first have to
step inside the mind of a frog.
Frogs and toads are built to react to motion.
In 1959, a famous study called
What the Frog's Eye Tells the Frog's
Brain found cells in the frog's
eye that respond strongly to small,
dark, moving objects.
It came from Jerome Lettvin and
his colleagues at MIT.
Later research on toads showed
that a part of the brain called
the optic tectum starts the turn
toward prey and the snap.
To a toad's brain,
something small that wiggles is food.
When researchers removed the tectum
in toads, the turn toward prey disappeared.
Researchers even found that toads
judge prey by its shape and its direction.
A thin object that moves along
its own length, like a worm crawling
forward, counts as food.
A millipede walking along its length
fits the same picture.
The same shape moving sideways
is usually ignored.
Scientists nicknamed these the
worm and the anti-worm.
The rules are fast,
and they work.
A frog does not need to think
about a fly.
It only needs to see the right
kind of movement.
In lab experiments, simple moving
dummies shaped like a worm were
enough to make toads turn and snap.
And that is exactly the weakness Epomis uses.
The Epomis larva sits still on
the ground and waits.
When a frog or toad comes near,
it starts to move its antennae
and its jaws.
Researchers call this luring.
To us, it looks like a strange little dance.
To a hungry frog,
it looks like a small creature
wriggling on the ground.
In other words, it looks like dinner.
The larva is not hiding from its predator.
It is calling it over.
Researchers measured this lure.
They moved a young green toad in
a small netted cage toward a larva,
step by step.
When the toad was fifteen centimeters
away, the larva made about 2.8
lure movements a minute.
When the toad was one centimeter
away, it made about 4.9.
With an empty cage,
it made only about one a minute.
The closer the predator came,
the harder the bait worked.
From the frog's point of view,
this is an easy meal.
It turns toward the movement,
creeps closer, and fixes both eyes
on its target.
That is the normal sequence for
a hunting toad: turn,
approach, fix, and snap.
The larva does not run,
and it does not hide in the leaf litter.
It keeps waving.
Every step brings the frog closer
to a moment its ancestors have
repeated countless times.
Except this time, the script has
been rewritten.
After a successful snap,
a toad swallows and often wipes
its mouth with a front foot.
Then the frog strikes.
Its sticky tongue flicks out in
less than a tenth of a second.
A 2017 study at the Georgia Institute
of Technology found that a frog's
tongue is about ten times softer
than a human tongue.
Its saliva turns runny on impact,
soaks into the prey,
and then thickens again as the
tongue pulls back.
Earlier research on horned frogs
measured a tongue pull of up to
1.4 times the frog's body weight.
Against a fly or a cricket,
that is usually the end of the story.
The tongue lands, the prey sticks,
and it vanishes into the frog's mouth.
Nature films have shown this moment
countless times.
But the Epomis larva is waiting
for exactly this moment.
What happens next is the reason
scientists filmed hundreds of these
encounters.
In almost every encounter,
the larva dodges the tongue.
Then, before the frog can react,
it latches on to the nearest part
of the amphibian's body,
usually around the mouth,
the throat, or the chest.
How does it time this so well?
The researchers wrote that the
mechanism of this swift counterattack
is still unknown.
Nobody knows exactly how a soft-bodied
larva times its escape so precisely.
What we do know is the result.
The predator has just become the prey.
Look closely at the larva's head,
and you can see why it does
not fall off.
Its jaws are unusual.
Each one ends in a double hook.
These double-hooked jaws are one
of the features that set Epomis larvae apart.
Once they are set into the frog's
skin, the larva hangs on,
and the hunt is over.
It is a little like a climber's
grappling hook, only on a creature
smaller than your thumb.
Now the larva starts to feed,
and it does so in two different ways.
A young larva feeds a lot like a parasite.
It sucks the frog's body fluids.
Many ground beetle larvae digest
food partly outside their bodies
before taking it in,
which may help explain how a tiny
larva can feed on something so big.
As the larva grows into its later
stages, it often switches from
sucking to chewing the tissue.
In other words, it starts as a
parasite and ends as a true predator.
The frog is much larger than the
larva, and yet it is the frog that disappears.
In the lab, the feeding ended with
the amphibian consumed, leaving
behind only a pile of bones.
Think about the scale.
An animal that hunts insects every
night is finished by an insect
smaller than a coin.
And for the larva,
this is not one lucky meal.
It is the plan for its whole childhood.
The researchers saw the same ending
again and again.
Once a larva had latched on,
the amphibian was eventually consumed.
Epomis larvae grow through three stages.
At the end of each stage,
the larva drops off its host and
molts in a hidden place.
Then it needs a new amphibian.
The studies we found do not say
how long each stage lasts.
So a single larva may have to
beat a frog or a toad three
times before it can grow up.
Each time, it uses the same trick:
wait, wave, dodge, and hook on.
Three hunts, three hosts,
and very little room for a mistake.
Why would any insect depend on
such a dangerous food?
Amphibians commonly eat ground beetles.
The researchers suggested that
this behavior may have started
as an extreme form of defense.
A larva that could survive an attack
had an advantage.
Over time, surviving the frog may
have turned into eating the frog.
It is a hypothesis,
not a proven history,
but it would explain why the larva's
whole life is built around the
animal that should eat it.
A similar interaction had also
been reported for another species,
Epomis nigricans, which hints that
the habit may run through more
of the genus.
For years, there were only scattered
reports of Epomis larvae found
clinging to amphibians in the wild.
Then, in 2011, two Israeli researchers,
Gil Wizen and Avital Gasith,
put the story to the test in the lab.
They used 420 larvae of two species,
Epomis circumscriptus and Epomis
dejeani, and five species of amphibians.
Their findings on the larvae appeared
in the journal PLoS ONE,
and a second paper on the adult
beetles appeared in ZooKeys.
Here is how a trial worked.
A single larva waited in a small
container, and then one young amphibian
was let in.
Each amphibian was used only once.
Video recording began ten seconds
before the amphibian arrived and
ran in ten-minute clips,
so the critical seconds were not missed.
Most trials used three kinds of
frogs and toads.
Newts and salamanders were rare,
so they were used only sparingly.
In total, the researchers used 420 larvae.
The results were striking.
The researchers ran 382 trials.
Only seven times did the amphibian
manage to gulp a larva,
and each time it quickly spat it back out.
In one more case,
a young toad actually swallowed a larva.
The larva stayed inside the toad's
stomach for about two hours.
Then the toad spat it out alive,
and the larva went on to attack
and eat the toad.
Almost every time, the amphibian lost.
These numbers come from lab containers,
where a frog and a larva cannot
walk away from each other.
In the wild, encounters may play
out differently, and the studies
do not give success rates from the field.
The amphibians in the trials were
young frogs and toads that had
only recently left the water,
not giant adults.
Even so, they were much larger
than the larva, and the method
worked almost every time.
Once its larval stages are done,
the larva goes on to become an adult beetle.
The adult is a striking animal,
about fifteen to twenty-six millimeters
long, often metallic blue or green,
with a yellow-orange rim along
its wing covers and yellow legs and antennae.
At first glance, it looks like
an ordinary ground beetle.
Inside the pupa, the soft body
of the larva has been rebuilt into
a hard, armored adult.
So does the frog hunting end with childhood?
It does not.
Adult Epomis beetles are generalist predators.
Beetles in their wider group are
known to eat other invertebrates
and even the carcasses of vertebrates.
But the Israeli researchers found
something more.
In the lab, adults also attacked
live amphibians: green toads,
Savigny's tree frogs, Levant water
frogs, banded newts, and fire salamanders.
Only one of the two species,
Epomis dejeani, ate the newts.
So the larva is a specialist,
and the adult is a generalist that
still hunts frogs.
Here is a strange detail.
During the day, adults of both
species share shelters with amphibians,
hiding under the same cover.
At night, the relationship changes.
Out in the field,
the researchers found beetles feeding
on green toads.
Attacks on the other amphibians
were seen only in the lab.
Imagine resting next to a neighbor
all day, without knowing that it
might be planning its dinner.
In another case reported from the
wild, three beetles were found
eating toads from behind.
The adult does not use a lure.
It uses an ambush.
In the lab, the beetle jumped onto
the amphibian's back and started
biting the lower back area.
The frog leaps and twists,
trying to throw it off,
but the beetle hangs on like a rodeo rider.
A frog's bulging eyes give it a
very wide view of the world,
but its tongue can only strike forward.
Against something riding on its
back, its best weapon is useless.
Then comes the bite that matters.
The beetle makes a horizontal cut
across the lower back of the amphibian.
Within about one to two minutes,
the animal stops moving.
A frog that cannot move cannot
escape, and a jump is its main way out.
After that, the beetle feeds,
chewing on the back and the sides.
Within a few hours,
only the head and the limbs remain.
You might guess that the beetle
simply cuts through the spinal cord.
But according to one of the researchers,
the cut does not harm the spine.
His leading idea is that the bite
damages the muscles that connect
the hind legs, but he says that
idea still needs to be confirmed.
So even the adult's signature move
holds a small mystery.
It clearly works, but no one has
yet proved exactly why.
Here is another puzzle.
Green toads, one of the beetle's
main victims, carry poison glands
in their skin, including two large
glands behind the eyes,
called parotoid glands.
These toxins protect toads from
many predators.
Yet Epomis larvae and adults attack
green toads anyway.
How they cope with the poison is
not explained in the studies we found.
Is the beetle resistant?
Does it simply avoid the glands?
No one knows for sure.
Lures are not unique to Epomis.
An anglerfish dangles a glowing
lure in the dark ocean,
a fin spine that has turned into
a fishing rod with a light at its tip.
An alligator snapping turtle lies
still with its mouth open and wiggles
a pink, wormlike tongue to draw fish inside.
But those predators are bigger
than their prey.
What makes Epomis so unusual is
that it lures an animal much bigger
than itself, an animal that is
supposed to be its predator,
and then survives the attack it invited.
Epomis is not the only small hunter
that breaks the size rules.
Praying mantises have been recorded
catching small birds.
A 2017 review collected 147 cases
in 13 countries, on every continent
except Antarctica.
The oldest report dates back to
1864, and the victims included
24 species of birds.
Most of the cases came from the
United States, and many involved
hummingbirds in gardens, where
the birds came to feeders or flowers.
A mantis ambushes, much like the
adult Epomis does.
Then there are the giant water bugs.
The largest species can grow more
than ten centimeters long,
longer than a baseball card.
Their young hunt tadpoles and small
fish, but adults take down prey
from fish to ducklings and even
venomous snakes.
They pierce their prey with a dagger-like
beak and inject enzymes that break
down its tissue, then suck the
liquid back up.
On large prey, a meal can take hours.
In 2019, the entomologist Shin-ya
Ohba reviewed these records.
Size, it turns out,
is not the same as rank.
So what is the lesson of the frog?
Its strength and its weakness are
the same thing.
Fast, simple rules let it catch
prey in a fraction of a second,
with no time to think.
Toads can learn to change what
they treat as prey,
but in the moment of the strike,
the rules decide.
A lure that moves like a worm
passes every test.
The larva does not break the frog's rules.
It follows them perfectly.
So where does all of this leave us?
Some big questions are still open.
No one knows exactly how the larva
times its dodge.
The adult's bite is thought to
damage the leg muscles,
but that idea has not been confirmed.
The poison of green toads does
not seem to stop the beetle,
and the studies do not say why.
And no one has measured how often
the larva wins in the wild.
A two-centimeter animal, and it
still keeps its secrets.
These beetles are hard to find.
They are small, the adults are
active at night, and the larvae
molt in hidden places between meals.
In Israel, the two species live
on the central coastal plain,
yet the researchers never found
them at the same site.
Across the Old World,
the genus is spread widely,
with most species in Africa.
Somewhere tonight, near a pond
you will never visit,
a larva may be waving its antennae
in the dark.
Next time you hear frogs calling
by a pond on a summer night,
listen a little longer.
It sounds peaceful.
But down in the wet leaves,
a two-centimeter hunter may be
waiting for one of those singers
to make the biggest mistake of its life.
Nature is full of these reversals,
where the hunter becomes the hunted
in a moment.
